render.text.justify.note: algorithm chosen; width measured over the OB, AP, DE and PR cells directly from the raw SAMPLE RECORD HTML (fixtures/SOURCES.md), decoding   to a plain space and removing exactly render5()'s own added indent for each row (1 leading space for continuation rows and for /PR's rows, 2 for the label row of a textBlock() call): every full-justified continuation line comes out to 65 characters; the widest line of all is the APPROACH label row at 66. Trial, 2026-09-09: reran render5.ts's own justify(text, width, stretch) algorithm in isolation against the sample's TI text and its OB/AP/PR narrative (reconstructed by collapsing each sample line's words to a single-spaced blob, since the visible multi-space runs in most sample lines are the full-justify stretching itself, then re-wrapping with the algorithm under test). At width 65, called directly for TI (not width - 1), TI's break reproduces the sample's exactly ('...DESIGNED TO' / 'MODIFY LIPID METABOLISM'). Every OB/AP/PR continuation line (28 of 30 checked rows, all of PR's 24 and all but the first row of OB and AP) also reproduces exactly at width 65. The two rows that do not match are the OBJECTIVES: and APPROACH: label rows themselves (63 and 66 measured characters respectively, not 65). Two causes fit that observation and neither is established: the sample may leave label rows unstretched (its OBJECTIVES: row is 63 characters, short of any width), or textBlock() glues the label into the word list it full-justifies so the label's trailing space is stretched like an inter-word gap. Either way the mismatch is unrelated to the width value, is present at any width, and is out of scope here since OB/AP/DE/PB/PR are not exercised by either given test (fixtures/bluesheet-sample-1998.txt marks them '# not-exercised'). Given the near-total reproduction and the TI break holding exactly, width 65 is adopted and TI's call is decoupled from width - 1 to width, called directly.

render.headings.join.claim: When a classification field carries more than one heading, the headings print joined by a semicolon and a space.

terminal.pacing.claim: Printed output arrives at 120 characters per second, a speed documented for DIALOG access in 1984-1988; no source records the speed of a File 60 session.

sources.locator: printed p. 28, section D, Online Communication: 30 or 120 characters per second as the common terminal speeds

ALIN v.14 no.3 (March 1988), printed p. 12, Karl Schneider, "Saving Search Money": "1200 baud or 120 bytes/sec" in a DIALOG print-cost model; "2400 baud access to DIALOG is now or will soon be available". Checked against the page image 2026-09-10.

terminal.pacing.note: Statement of absence: the speed of any 1990-1994 File 60 session was not found by a search of this project's sources, a search of the 89 ALIN OCR files, and one web search, on 2026-09-10. The sources cited here state speeds at which DIALOG was reached in and around the anchor period; none of them is a record of a File 60 session, and the anchor-period sources it consulted are printouts, which record no timing. 120 characters per second is chosen from that documented range, not measured from any session. src/terminal/sink.ts reads cps from this value and emits printed characters at that rate. The ALIN v.15 no.1 (1989) dial-in figure (1200 or 2400 baud) was checked against the page image on 2026-09-10 and is the access speed of ALF, NAL's bulletin board, not of DIALOG; it is not cited here. The prompt stays live during output: src/terminal/sink.ts never disables the input while a line paces out at this rate, and a line entered before the output finishes is taken up once it does.

terminal.line_editing.value: native single-line editing: character insert, backspace, left and right, paste; no history
terminal.line_editing.claim: Typing uses the browser's own text editing: insert, backspace, arrows, paste. Enter submits the line. This is not a simulation of a period terminal's editing.
terminal.line_editing.note: What a 1990 searcher could edit before return is not recorded in any source held; the textarea covers insert, backspace, arrows and paste. The textarea's native editing is the input model, not a simulation of a documented DIALOG editing rule. Enter submission is the app's, not the textarea's own behaviour, and the visible caret is drawn by the app (index.html's caret-color:transparent and the .cursor span); the editing itself is the browser's.

terminal.wrap.claim: A long set line wraps in the browser rather than running off the edge; no source documents how DIALOG itself wrapped long lines.

terminal.scrollback.value: the browser's own scrollbar; no custom scroll chrome
terminal.scrollback.claim: The session stays on screen and can be scrolled back; a 1990s terminal did not keep it.
terminal.scrollback.note: DIALOG sent a character stream. On a printing terminal, output was printed and could not be scrolled back; on a screen it scrolled off the top unless the searcher's own communications program buffered it, which no source in the corpus records.

index.format.value: one JSON file per phrase-indexed field, offsets.json for record spans
index.format.claim: Search terms are looked up in files built for this reconstruction; how DIALOG itself indexed File 60 internally is not known.
index.format.note: DIALOG's own internal index structures are unknown to us; this is a search accelerator built for this reconstruction, not a claim about how DIALOG indexed File 60

inspect.mode.value: click-to-inspect panel: What was printed, How DIALOG names it, The bytes in the NARA file, Where the file came from, Why it prints this way
inspect.mode.claim: Clicking a printed line opens a panel explaining how that line was produced, back to its position in the archival file.
inspect.mode.note: Inspect mode is modern scholarly apparatus with no DIALOG-period precedent. The panel's cards are named for a reader: the record's Format B bytes and its archival container are one card, "The bytes in the NARA file"; the rest are "What was printed", "How DIALOG names it", "Where the file came from" (tape provenance) and "Why it prints this way" (transformation evidence). The panel can be hidden behind a toggle at the aside's edge; hiding it changes nothing in the session -- it is a display choice over the same character stream.

terminal.keyboard_inspect.value: stamped spans are tabbable; Enter/Space opens inspect; Escape returns focus to the prompt; Alt+I inspects the most recent typed record line
terminal.keyboard_inspect.claim: The inspect panel can also be reached from the keyboard: Tab to a line and press Enter, or press Alt+I for the line typed most recently.
terminal.keyboard_inspect.note: Keyboard-only operation for a mouse-only affordance (click-to-inspect) that DIALOG itself never had, so there is no DIALOG-period rule this could be inferred from.

terminal.restart.value: a button (and Alt+R) discards the session's sets and open file, empties the printout and inspect panel, and returns to an empty prompt
terminal.restart.claim: A button restarts the session; in the period a searcher logged off and dialed in again.
terminal.restart.note: DIALOG had no clear command; ending a session and starting another meant LOGOFF, then dialing in again. Restart is implemented as app wiring (src/app/main.ts constructs a fresh DialogSession and calls DomSink.reset()), not a DIALOG-layer concept, and it prints nothing into the character stream -- no LOGOFF accounting block (not implemented) and no new BEGIN banner, since neither corresponds to any DIALOG output this control actually causes.

index.word.tokens.value: split on spaces and on punctuation other than the hyphen; digits are tokens; keys are uppercased
index.word.tokens.claim: A search term is split at spaces and punctuation other than the hyphen; digits count as terms; everything is matched in capitals.
index.word.tokens.decision: the 2001 book states what a word-indexed search term may contain (any single word, number, or alphanumeric expression) and that punctuation inside one must be replaced with a proximity operator to search it; this reconstruction reads that as punctuation not being part of the indexed token and drops it at split time, rather than indexing the punctuation character itself, which is the alternative it does not adopt.

index.word.stopwords.claim: Nine common words (an, by, for, from, of, the, to, with, and) are never indexed as search terms.

sources.locator: page 206, the nine Dialog stop words (lines 21687-21709)

index.word.stopwords.note: the 2001 book documents this list for DIALOG generally, not for File 60 in 1994 specifically; that it held for the 1994 export is inferred, not itself documented for that year.

index.word.hyphen.value: indexed whole and as its parts
index.word.hyphen.claim: A hyphenated word is indexed as one term and as each of its parts, so a search can match either.
index.word.hyphen.decision: indexed whole (e.g. GENE-TRANSFER) and as its parts (GENE, TRANSFER); the alternative, whole only, is not adopted. No source held states which DIALOG itself did.

index.word.shards.value: one file per first character: A-Z, 0-9, and _ for anything else
index.word.shards.claim: The word lists are split into files by first letter so a search loads only the part it needs; DIALOG's own index shape is not known.

index.word.positions.claim: Where each word sits in each field is recorded so that searches for words near each other can be answered.
index.word.positions.note:
Statement of absence: how DIALOG itself stored or counted word positions is not found by grepping 'position', 'adjacen' and 'proximity' across the 2001 manual text and the stripped 1998 Blue Sheet text on 2026-09-10, and by reading the 1988 figures and the 1978 session. Everything below is this reconstruction's own chosen mechanism, not a reading of a held source.

Packing: a packed position is fieldOrdinal * FIELD_STRIDE + wordPosition, one integer per occurrence rather than a two-element array -- fieldOrdinal is the field's index among that code's occurrences in the record (so two values of a repeating tag, or a composite code's second component tag, are two field ordinals, never one -- a word in /TX's AP and a word in its OB do not share a field ordinal, so (F) cannot wrongly join them); wordPosition is the word's 0-based position within that field's text.

Stop-word counting: positions are counted over every whitespace-separated word of a field, including the nine stop words (index.word.stopwords), even though a stop word itself is never posted. This keeps 'adjacent in the text' meaning what it says across a dropped stop word -- FRESH WATER and FRESH THE WATER must not both look adjacent, which they would if position counting skipped stop words the way the word-index tokenizer (index.word.tokens) does.

Hyphen rule: a hyphenated token (index.word.hyphen) posts its whole form and each part at the SAME packed position -- they are one word of the field, indexed three ways, not three consecutive words; a proximity operator must see one position for GENE-TRANSFER's occurrence, not GENE at one position and TRANSFER at the next.

FIELD_STRIDE: measured 2026-09-11 (python3 over data/RG164.CRIS.FY94.txt, 277,539,004 bytes, the same script recorded in docs/indexes.md) as the longest of the TI/OB/AP/PR/DE/PB fields across the FY 1994 corpus in whitespace-separated words, including stop words: 296. FIELD_STRIDE is the next power of two above that, 512 -- comfortably above the measured maximum, so no field's word positions can overflow into the next field ordinal.

Which codes ship (decision (a), Trevor's pre-approved rule): buildIndexes() (src/loader/index-builder.ts) takes which codes to build positions for as an argument, defaulting to POSITIONAL_CODES (src/loader/words.ts) -- /TI and /DE, the only codes src/loader/cli.ts writes and scripts/upload-corpus.sh uploads. A one-time run passing every WORD_CODES entry (2026-09-11, `pnpm load` against the full 277,539,004-byte corpus, 34,090 records) measured the full eight-code positional index at 205,241,665 bytes under public/corpus/pos -- over this reconstruction's 150 MB ceiling on bytes added to the bucket's v1/ prefix -- which is what set the default to the smaller subset: version 1 ships positions for only the two Basic Index codes /TI and /DE, 16,883,977 of those bytes. /TX, /AP, /OB, /PR, /PB and PO= carry no positional index; docs/not-implemented.md records proximity over them as not implemented, with this measurement as the stated reason. Computing all eight unconditionally on every buildIndexes() call, the first version of this loader, also pushed several archival tests that build fresh over the real corpus past Vitest's 60s per-file RPC timeout -- a second reason the default stays narrow; test/regression/positional-index.test.ts passes the full WORD_CODES list explicitly, since its composite-code check needs /TX and it runs only against the tiny committed fixture record. Full one-time measurement, per code (occurrences, on-disk bytes): /TI 253,982 / 3,258,188; /OB 1,380,885 / 15,624,681; /AP 2,374,933 / 25,651,311; /DE 1,214,193 / 13,625,789; /PR 4,161,495 / 43,133,386; /PB 1,794,984 / 18,495,289; /TX 7,917,313 / 83,279,393; PO= 169,491 / 2,173,628.

map.TX.composite.claim: The TX search field merges three fields' text on this corpus; the Blue Sheet documents a fourth this corpus never carries.
map.TX.composite.note: the Blue Sheet's footnote 6 documents /TX as the union of /AP, /NR, /OB and /PR. /NR is the HNRIMS narrative tag NA; its FY 1994 count in this corpus is 0 (measured, index-builder.ts's word-index build), so on this corpus /TX is built as AP + OB + PR. The missing /NR component is a consequence of the corpus, not a choice made here.

index.sh.phrase_only.value: SH= built as a phrase index only
index.sh.phrase_only.claim: Subject headings are searched as whole phrases only; one source calls two of their fields word-searchable, a reading not adopted here.

sources.locator: elements 46 and 47 (PH, GH): 'Word and Phrase', SH= 'searches literal only'

index.sh.phrase_only.conflicts: Format B's own element table calls PH and GH 'Word and Phrase' under SH=, while its entry for SH= itself says the field 'searches literal only', i.e. phrase-indexed. The phrase-only reading is what this build implements; the disagreement is recorded here rather than resolved silently.

terminal.width_rule.claim: A thin vertical line marks the 80-column edge of the printout; the terminals drew no such line. It is hidden when the window is narrower than the printout.
terminal.width_rule.note: The documented terminals were width-limited (terminal.width, 80 columns) and a modern browser window is wider, so the printout's right edge is marked with the same neutral rule colour the panels use. index.html .printout{border-right} and the @container query on .terminal-pane enact it; no colour or CRT claim is made. Chosen: a modern convenience with no historical counterpart.

proto.select.precedence.claim: Without brackets, NOT is worked out first, then AND, then OR; brackets change the order, innermost first.

sources.locator: SELECT, "Logical and Proximity Operators" / "Order of Processing"

proto.select.precedence.decision: no anchor-period source states the order of processing, so this reconstruction follows the 2001 book's stated order (parentheses, then proximity, then NOT, then AND, then OR) instead of refusing mixed operators.
proto.select.precedence.note: As of Task 8, (W), (N), (F) and their numbered forms (nW)/(nN) are implemented and exercise the proximity step of this order; (S), (L) and (T) are refused (proto.select.proximity.unimplemented) and never reach it.

proto.select.boolean.claim: Searches can be combined with AND, OR and NOT; NOT takes a set on each side and cannot start a statement.

sources.locator: p. 185, "? COMBINE (8 AND 12) NOT 15" answered "16 35 (8 AND 12) NOT 15"

proto.select.boolean.decision: NOT is binary (spec 7.12); a leading NOT does not parse. In 1978 these combinations were made with COMBINE and a set-number legend, not SELECT's own AND/OR/NOT words; COMBINE is out of this slice, and the SELECT form of 1984 onward is what this reconstruction implements.

proto.select.proximity.claim: Three proximity operators are implemented: (W) requires two terms next to each other in the order typed, (N) the same but in either order, and (F) only that both terms are in the same field.

sources.locator: Basic Index, SELECT examples: 'S SERUM(W)LIPID?/DE', 'S FISH(F)OIL?/NR', 'S LIPID?(N)LEVEL?/OB', 'S LIPID?(3N)METABOL?/TI'; Additional Indexes, 'S PO=(OHIO(W)STATE)'

SELECT, "Logical and Proximity Operators": (W) 'Requests that terms be adjacent to each other and in the order specified.'; (N) 'Requests that terms be adjacent but in any order.'; (F) 'Requests that terms be in the same field, as defined by the database.'

p. 99 (printed 113), 'Uso de los operadores de proximidad (W), (), y (N)': '?ss technolog?(w)transfer?/ti' -> 'S1 4322 TECHNOLOG?/TI', 'S2 1330 TRANSFER?/TI', 'S3 252 TECHNOLOG?(W)TRANSFER?/TI' (File 49, Pais Int., not File 60, but the same DIALOG SELECT/SS mechanics: a single trailing suffix shared by both truncated operands, and one per-operand set line before the combined one)

proto.select.proximity.decision: (S), (L) and (T) are not implemented -- each is defined only relative to something 'as defined by the database' (a subfield unit, a descriptor unit, or a chemical name's parts), and no held source states what any of those three are for File 60. Implementing them would mean choosing a definition and presenting it as File 60's own. Statement of absence: not found by grepping "(S)", "(L)", "(T)", "subfield", "descriptor unit" and "chemical name" across the stripped 1998 Blue Sheet text and Successful_Searching_on_Dialog_2001_djvu.txt on 2026-09-10. A SELECT using one of the three parses to null, the same as any other statement this grammar cannot read (proto.select.proximity.unimplemented carries the runtime-facing side of this same absence).
proto.select.proximity.note: Resolved over the positional index Task 7 built, which ships positions for /TI and /DE only -- a proximity SELECT naming any other code (/TX, /AP, /OB, /PR, /PB, PO=) is refused at prepare() time (UnimplementedProximityField) and routed to the capability-notice channel, not silently accepted; see proto.select.proximity.unimplemented and index.word.positions for the 150 MB ceiling that set that boundary.

proto.select.proximity.numbered.value: n is the maximum distance between the two terms' word positions; adjacent terms are distance 1, so at most n-1 words may fall between them
proto.select.proximity.numbered.claim: A number before (W) or (N), like (3N), sets n as the max distance between the two terms' word positions; adjacent is distance 1.

sources.locator: SELECT worked example: '?s self(Iw)esteem and kindergarten?' (the OCR renders '(1W)' as '(Iw)')

proto.select.proximity.numbered.decision: No held source states what the number in (nW)/(nN) means -- only the examples (1W), (2N) (implicit in the 1994 Curso's own bare-(W)-vs-(1N) pairing, where (1N)'s count 382 differs from (W)'s 252) and (3N) appear. This reconstruction's near() reads n as the maximum allowed distance between the two terms' word positions -- adjacent terms are distance 1, so a bare (W)/(N) requires adjacency (0 words between) and (nW)/(nN) allows at most n-1 intervening words. That meaning is this reconstruction's inferred reading, chosen because no held source defines it; the alternative reading (n as the count of intervening words directly) is not adopted.

proto.select.proximity.perterm.value: one postings line per word, then one for the proximity expression, then the set line
proto.select.proximity.perterm.claim: A proximity search prints a count for each word searched, then a count for the whole proximity expression, then the set line -- the same shape any other multi-term search prints.

sources.locator: SELECT worked example: '?s self(Iw)esteem and kindergarten?' -> '223646 SELF', '26261 ESTEEM', '25506 SELF(IW)ESTEEM', '19458 KINDERGARTEN?', 'S2 265 SELF(IW)ESTEEM AND KINDERGARTEN?'
a (W) expression's printed postings lines with SET DETAIL off, the same shape
p. 99 (printed 113): 'S1 4322 TECHNOLOG?/TI', 'S2 1330 TRANSFER?/TI', 'S3 252 TECHNOLOG?(W)TRANSFER?/TI' -- SELECT STEPS' own per-operand-then-combined numbering, applied to a proximity expression

proto.select.proximity.perterm.decision: No new printing rule: the existing perTerm mechanism (one line per leaf, in evaluation order, then the combined/set line) already produces this shape; the proximity node contributes its own line after its operands' lines. Moved from a 2001-only bracket to a 1994-anchored reading once the Curso p. 99 render (Task 8 Step 1) turned out legible.

proto.select.proximity.unimplemented.claim: Three of DIALOG's proximity operators are refused here, because no surviving source says what they meant in this file.
proto.select.proximity.unimplemented.note: Statement of absence: no File 60 definition of the (S), (L) or (T) units is found by grepping "(S)", "(L)", "(T)", "subfield", "descriptor unit" and "chemical name" across the stripped 1998 Blue Sheet text and Successful_Searching_on_Dialog_2001_djvu.txt on 2026-09-10 (see proto.select.proximity's own decision for the same absence, stated once and cited from both). Separately, and for a different reason: proximity over any Basic Index code other than /TI and /DE -- /TX, /AP, /OB, /PR, /PB, and PO= -- is also not implemented, because the positional index Task 7 built ships only /TI and /DE (the full eight-code positional index measured 205,241,665 bytes, over this reconstruction's 150 MB ceiling on bytes added to the bucket's v1/ prefix, Trevor's pre-approved decision (a), recorded at index.word.positions). A proximity SELECT naming an unshipped code is refused at prepare() time (UnimplementedProximityField, src/retrieval/engine.ts) and routed to the capability-notice channel, the same as any other documented-but-unimplemented File 60 search -- never silently accepted as a zero-item set.

proto.select.truncation.claim: A question mark at the end of a search word finds every word that starts with it, counted together on one line.

sources.locator: Basic Index, SELECT examples: 'S DIET?/PR', 'S CHOLESTEROL?/TX'
Sample Search/Output, p. 184: '? SELECT LOBSTER?' printing '3 14 LOBSTER?'

proto.select.truncation.note: Only the single trailing '?' is implemented. Statement of absence: no other truncation form (bounded '??', spaced '? ?', internal '?') was found for File 60 by grepping 'truncat', '??' and '? ?' across the 2001 manual text and the stripped 1998 Blue Sheet text on 2026-09-10; the parser refuses those forms rather than reading them as a single '?'.
